# MLL1 Inhibition Reprograms Epiblast Stem Cells to Naive Pluripotency.

The interconversion between naive and primed pluripotent states is accompanied by drastic epigenetic rearrangements. However, it is unclear whether intrinsic epigenetic events can drive reprogramming to naive pluripotency or if distinct chromatin states are instead simply a reflection of discrete pluripotent states. Here, we show that blocking histone H3K4 methyltransferase MLL1 activity with the small-molecule inhibitor MM-401 reprograms mouse epiblast stem cells (EpiSCs) to naive pluripotency. This reversion is highly efficient and synchronized, with more than 50% of treated EpiSCs exhibiting features of naive embryonic stem cells (ESCs) within 3 days. Reverted ESCs reactivate the silenced X chromosome and contribute to embryos following blastocyst injection, generating germline-competent chimeras. Importantly, blocking MLL1 leads to global redistribution of H3K4me1 at enhancers and represses lineage determinant factors and EpiSC markers, which indirectly regulate ESC transcription circuitry. These findings show that discrete perturbation of H3K4 methylation is sufficient to drive reprogramming to naive pluripotency.

Inhibitory histone methyltransferases (HMTs) impose gene-specific gatekeeper functions preventing unliganded nuclear receptors from binding target promoters, requiring demethylases including LSD1 for ligand/signal-dependent activation—circumventing pathological constitutive gene induction. In bovine somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT), eight-cell embryos show global hypermethylation of H3K9me3/2; H3K9 demethylases KDM4D and KDM4E mediate active demethylation in IVF embryos but are deficient in cloned embryos at embryonic genome activation (EGA). KDM4E is more crucial: its overexpression restores the transcriptome, improves blastocyst formation and cloning efficiency, and RNA–KDM4E interactions are essential for H3K9 demethylation during EGA. Finally, base-pair-resolution mouse methylomes in stem cells and neuronal progenitors reveal low-methylated regions (LMRs) averaging 30% methylation, representing CpG-poor distal regulatory regions shaped by DNA-binding factors.

Inhibitory histone methyltransferases (HMTs) act as gene-specific gatekeepers, preventing unliganded nuclear receptors from binding target promoters and requiring demethylases such as LSD1 for ligand/signal-dependent activation, thereby circumventing pathological constitutive gene induction. In bovine somatic cell nuclear transfer (SCNT), eight-cell embryos display global hypermethylation of H3K9me3/2; the H3K9 demethylases KDM4D and KDM4E mediate active demethylation in IVF embryos but are deficient in cloned embryos at embryonic genome activation (EGA). KDM4E is the more crucial factor: its overexpression restores the transcriptome, improves blastocyst formation and cloning efficiency, and RNA–KDM4E interactions are essential for H3K9 demethylation during EGA. Finally, base-pair-resolution mouse methylomes in stem cells and neuronal progenitors reveal low-methylated regions (LMRs) averaging 30% methylation—CpG-poor distal regulatory regions shaped by DNA-binding factors.

# Induction of pluripotent stem cells by defined factors is greatly improved by small-molecule compounds

Reprogramming of mouse and human somatic cells can be achieved by ectopic expression of transcription factors, but with low efficiencies. We report that DNA methyltransferase and histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors improve reprogramming efficiency. In particular, valproic acid (VPA), an HDAC inhibitor, improves reprogramming efficiency by more than 100-fold, using Oct4-GFP as a reporter. VPA also enables efficient induction of pluripotent stem cells without introduction of the oncogene c-Myc.

# Reprogramming of human fibroblasts to pluripotency with lineage specifiers.

Since the initial discovery that OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and c-MYC overexpression sufficed for the induction of pluripotency in somatic cells, methodologies replacing the original factors have enhanced our understanding of the reprogramming process. However, unlike in mouse, OCT4 has not been replaced successfully during reprogramming of human cells. Here we report on a strategy to accomplish this replacement. Through a combination of transcriptome and bioinformatic analysis we have identified factors previously characterized as being lineage specifiers that are able to replace OCT4 and SOX2 in the reprogramming of human fibroblasts. Our results show that it is possible to replace OCT4 and SOX2 simultaneously with alternative lineage specifiers in the reprogramming of human cells. At a broader level, they also support a model in which counteracting lineage specification networks underlies the induction of pluripotency.

Reprogramming human somatic cells to pluripotency was first achieved with OCT4, SOX2, KLF4, and c-MYC. Subsequent work replaced original factors, but OCT4 had not been successfully substituted in human cells, unlike in mouse. Using transcriptome and bioinformatic analysis, researchers identified lineage-specifier factors able to replace OCT4 and SOX2 in reprogramming human fibroblasts. Results show OCT4 and SOX2 can be replaced simultaneously by alternative lineage specifiers, supporting a model in which counteracting lineage-specification networks underlie pluripotency induction. Separately, DNA methyltransferase and histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors improve reprogramming efficiency; valproic acid (VPA), an HDAC inhibitor, boosts efficiency over 100-fold (using Oct4-GFP reporter) and enables efficient induction of pluripotent stem cells without the oncogene c-Myc.

The midbody is an organelle formed between daughter cells during cytokinesis, required for their final separation. Midbody derivatives (MBds) persist long after division, with unclear fate. MBds are inherited asymmetrically by the daughter cell with the older centrosome and selectively accumulate in stem cells, induced pluripotent stem cells and potential cancer 'stem cells' in vivo and in vitro. MBd loss accompanies stem-cell differentiation, involving autophagic degradation mediated by NBR1 binding to CEP55. Differentiating and normal dividing cells do not accumulate MBds and have high autophagic activity, whereas stem and cancer cells accumulate MBds by evading autophagosome encapsulation and show low autophagic activity. MBd enrichment enhances reprogramming to induced pluripotent stem cells and increases in vitro tumorigenicity of cancer cells, indicating unexpected roles in stem cells and cancer 'stem cells'.

Three papers. (1) FASEB J 2001 (10.1096/fj.00-0815fje): cholesterol is essential for synaptic plasticity and neuronal degeneration; ex vivo cholesterol efflux induced by human CSF-HDL3 and methyl-β-cyclodextrin impairs short- and long-term plasticity in adult rat hippocampal slices (CA1 fEPSPs). (2) ATM deficiency causes nuclear HDAC4 accumulation in neurons, driving ataxia-telangiectasia neurodegeneration; nuclear HDAC4 binds chromatin, MEF2A and CREB, altering gene expression. Blocking HDAC4 activity or nuclear accumulation rescues ATM-deficient mouse behaviors, though full rescue requires cytoplasmic HDAC4; ATM phosphorylation downregulates PP2A, excess activity of which dephosphorylates HDAC4. (3) Osteoblast-secreted PGE2 activates sensory-nerve EP4, inhibiting sympathetic activity via the CNS to regulate bone formation; PGE2 rises as bone density falls in osteoporotic models, and sensory nerve ablation erodes skeletal integrity.
